newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont jury asks for judge's homicide explanation.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont jury asks for judge's homicide explanation.

text.p: Jurors deliberating in the murder trial of John du Pont on Wednesday asked the judge to repeat her explanation of the differing degrees of homicide the millionaire chemicals heir is charged with.

On their second day of deliberations, which focus on du Pont's state of mind when he killed Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz in January 1996, the jury also asked for a re-reading of key testimony from a witness to the shooting.

It also requested a map of the route du Pont, 58, took to Schultz's house on the du Pont estate and chart exhibits on factors pertinent to whether du Pont knew that what he was doing was wrong, the key issue in his insanity defence.

In her instructions before the jury began deliberations on Tuesday afternoon, Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins said the jury, if it concluded du Pont shot Schultz, must then decide whether he was innocent by reason of insanity before considering the various degrees of homicide.

The jury could also deliver a verdict of not guilty or guilty or guilty but mentally ill on any one of the three degrees of homicide du Pont has been charged with -- first degree and third degree murder and voluntary manslaughter.
Jenkins reiterated for the jury that first-degree murder required a specific intent to kill and legal malice on the part of the killer.
Du Pont's lawyers have conceded he killed Schultz but said he was legally insane at the time.

A court official read for the jury testimony of security consultant Patrick Goodale, who rode in du Pont's car to Schultz's house. Included in the testimony were statements by Goodale that du Pont had previously agreed not to carry weapons in the presence of security company employees but brought a gun with him on that drive.
This could support prosecution contentions that du Pont planned to kill Schultz.

But the testimony also contained Goodale's statement to investigators that du Pont's "speed and decisiveness" in shooting Schultz was surprising and uncharacteristic of his way of dealing with anger. This could support defence contentions the killing was spontaneous.

If the jury finds du Pont guilty but mentally ill he would face the same penalties as an ordinary guilty verdict but could receive psychiatric treatment before serving the rest of his sentence. A hearing on how to treat him would be held.
If he is found not guilty by reason of insanity, a hearing would immediately be held on whether du Pont should be treated in a psychiatric hospital or freed.
